239.title: The peacemakers (Matthew 5:9)
239.hook: peacemakers, not peacekeepers: they make peace where there wasn't any
239.carry: make peace, not just keep it
239.howItsDone: Christians work at peacemaking through mediation between neighbors and reconciliation between communities; for the historic peace churches, such as Mennonites and Quakers, it sits at the center of their life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, katharos: clean, unmixed, a single heart. Your line was a single heart sees.

Plenty of families have a peacekeeper. The one who changes the subject when politics comes up at dinner. Who says, let's not get into it. Who smooths things over so nobody storms out. It's a real gift, and often an exhausting one. But under a kept peace, the problem is often still there. The two brothers still aren't speaking. The old hurt still sits in the corner. The seventh line of the sermon doesn't bless the peacekeepers. It uses a different word.
screen: `THE FAMILY PEACEKEEPER.` → `LET'S NOT GET INTO IT.` → `A DIFFERENT WORD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The Greek word is eirenopoioi. Eirene is peace; poieo is to make, to build. Peace-makers: people who build a peace that wasn't there before. And behind it is the Hebrew shalom. Shalom isn't just no fighting. It's wholeness: everything in its right place, nothing missing, nothing broken. So a peacemaker doesn't just stop the shouting. They go into the broken place and help build something whole. That's harder. It usually means naming what's wrong, listening to both sides, and taking some heat, often from both sides at once. And remember the world Jesus said this in: a land under Rome, whose Pax Romana, the Roman peace, was kept by legions and crosses. Jesus blesses a different kind: peace that's made, not enforced. The promise: they shall be called the children of God. In Hebrew idiom, the son of something shares its character. Peacemakers are called God's children because they're doing what, Christians say, God does: making peace between people who were apart. Paul would later put the practical version this way: "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men." It takes two to make peace. But you can do your half.

segments.voice: Think of a relationship with a quiet cold war, not a battle, just a chill: someone you avoid, something unsaid. Picture them and ask what your half of making peace would be: an apology, asking are we okay, a friendly message after a long silence, the smallest real step. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for courage.
The peacemakers. Eirenopoioi, peace builders: people who make shalom where there wasn't any, and are called the children of God.
Your line: make peace, not just keep it. A peacemaker builds; a peacekeeper smooths. See you on the hillside tomorrow.

240.title: Persecuted (Matthew 5:10–12)
240.hook: blessed when you're insulted for doing right
240.howItsDone: Christians remember martyrs on their feast days, and many churches set aside a day or a Sunday each year to pray for Christians who are persecuted around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peacemakers: people who build peace where there wasn't any. Your line was make peace, not just keep it.

Sometimes doing right costs you. You speak up for someone and get frozen out of the group. You tell the truth and lose the deal. You refuse to laugh at the joke and become the next joke. Doing right doesn't always get applause. Sometimes it gets punished. The last of the Beatitudes is the one nobody puts on a coffee mug. After the empty-handed, the mourners, the meek, the hungry, the merciful, the pure and the peacemakers, Jesus blesses the people who get hurt for it.
screen: `IT COST YOU.` → `THE NEXT JOKE.` → `THE LAST BEATITUDE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Listen to that ending. It's the same promise as the very first beatitude, the poor in spirit. The list opens and closes with the same words, like bookends, and everything in between lives inside the kingdom. And notice: for righteousness' sake. Not for being difficult, or rude, or right in an annoying way. For doing what's right. Then Jesus speaks straight to the people in front of him, not they any more but ye: blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Then comes the strangest instruction in the sermon: "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you." The Greek for be exceeding glad, agalliasthe, is more than smiling through it. It's the word for jumping for joy. Why rejoice? Not because pain is good. Because you're in good company: the prophets walked this road before you. The book of Acts tells how the apostles, after being beaten, left rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for his name. Christians have been persecuted in many times and places, from the first centuries to today, and people of many faiths know that suffering too. In the second century, Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed: the more Christians were killed, the more the church grew. For people in that position, this beatitude is not a nice saying. It's a promise that their story doesn't end in the cell.

segments.voice: Around the world, some Christians face prison, violence or losing their homes for what they believe; picture one of them: a pastor in a cell, a family that had to flee, a teenager mocked at school for praying. If you pray, you can pray for them now, by name if you know one. If you don't pray, simply hold them in mind, and wish them courage and safety.
Persecuted. The last beatitude: blessed are those hurt for doing right, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

241.title: Salt and light (Matthew 5:13–16)
241.hook: you are the salt of the earth, the light of the world
241.howItsDone: In Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and some other baptisms, a candle is lit and given to the newly baptized as a sign that they are to be light in the world, and Christians often use salt and light as pictures for living their faith in ordinary places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last beatitude: blessed are those hurt for doing right, in the company of the prophets. Your line was rejoice anyway.

She's the salt of the earth. People still say it about a grandmother, a neighbor, the guy at the hardware store: someone solid, honest, no fuss. Plenty of people who say it don't know they're quoting Jesus. Right after the Beatitudes, Jesus turns to the disciples who came near him on the hillside, ordinary people, and tells them two things about who they are. Not who they should become someday. Who they already are.
screen: `SALT OF THE EARTH.` → `QUOTING JESUS WITHOUT KNOWING.` → `WHO THEY ALREADY ARE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?" In a world without refrigerators, salt was precious. It kept fish and meat from rotting. It brought out flavor. A little of it changed everything around it. But salt can lose its savor. Some readers explain that salt gathered from marshes was mixed with other minerals; if the real salt washed out, what was left looked like salt and did nothing. And there's a detail in the Greek: the verb for lose its savor is moraino, a verb that can also mean to become foolish. Salt that's lost its saltiness has, in a sense, gone foolish. Then the second picture: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." Picture a village on a Galilean hillside at night, its lamps glowing, visible for miles. Nobody, Jesus says, lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel basket. You put it on a stand so it lights the whole house. Then the line that ties it together: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Notice where the credit goes. Not so they see how good you are. So they glorify your Father. The light isn't a spotlight on you; it's a lamp that helps other people see. And notice the tense again. Not you should try to be light. Ye are.

segments.voice: Think of a small good thing you could do that someone else would notice: helping a coworker in the open, thanking someone in front of others, holding a door and actually smiling. Not to be admired, just to put a little light on the stand so someone else can see by it. If you pray, you can offer it to God ahead of time.

242.title: Not to abolish (Matthew 5:17–20)
242.hook: he came to fulfill the law and the prophets, not to destroy them
242.howItsDone: Christians read the Old Testament in worship alongside the Gospels, and in churches that follow a lectionary, a Sunday service often includes a reading from the law or the prophets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moraino: salt that's lost its savor has, in a sense, gone foolish. Your line was you are the light.

Some people picture Jesus throwing out the old rulebook. Out with the laws, in with love. It's a popular idea, and it's the very thing Jesus heads off next in the sermon. His listeners were crowds from Galilee, Jerusalem and Judea, people who knew the Torah from the synagogue. Some may have wondered: is this new teacher against it? Before he says anything else, he answers.
screen: `THROW OUT THE OLD RULEBOOK?` → `CROWDS WHO KNEW THE TORAH.` → `BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, HE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." The law here is the Torah, the first five books of the Bible, Genesis to Deuteronomy. Torah is usually translated law, but the Hebrew word means more like teaching, or instruction: the way God shows people how to live. For Jews it's the heart of scripture, and it still is. Then: till heaven and earth pass, "one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled." A jot is the yod, a Hebrew letter hardly bigger than an apostrophe. A tittle is a tiny stroke, the little hook that tells one Hebrew letter from another. Not even that much will be lost. So what does fulfill mean? Christians read it several ways. Some say Jesus fulfills the law by living it completely and bringing out its deepest intent, which the rest of the chapter goes on to do. Some also say parts of it, like the temple sacrifices, find their fulfillment in him. Churches differ on exactly how the law applies to Christians today, and Jews, for their part, continue to live by the Torah as their covenant with God. Then: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. In his day the Pharisees were known for taking the law seriously, down to the details. He isn't lowering the bar. He's saying: go deeper, all the way to the heart.

segments.voice: The words Jesus means are, first of all, the Torah, still read, sung and studied in synagogues week by week. Think of a Jewish neighbor, friend or coworker, or Jewish families you've never met, gathering around those same scrolls, and hold them in mind with respect and gratitude. If you pray, you can give thanks for the Torah and for the people who have carried it through the generations.
Torah. The first five books of the Bible; in Hebrew, not just law, but teaching: the way to live. Jesus says he came not to destroy it.
Your line: fulfill, not destroy. Not one jot or tittle of it will be lost, he says. See you tomorrow.

243.title: Anger (Matthew 5:21–26)
243.hook: before you bring your gift, go and be reconciled
243.howItsDone: In churches that share the peace during the service, it often comes before the gifts are brought to the altar or before communion, a custom some link to this passage, and some Christians make a point of mending quarrels before receiving communion or before Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah: teaching, the way to live. Jesus came not to destroy it, but to fulfill it.

Thou shalt not kill. It sounds like a commandment almost anyone could keep. But then there's the name muttered under the breath at a brother or sister. The furious speech rehearsed in the shower, to someone who isn't there. Walking into church, a family dinner or a meeting while someone in the room is still upset, and just carrying on. Jesus has said: go deeper, to the heart. Now he shows what that means, starting with one of the Ten Commandments.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT KILL.` → `A FURIOUS SPEECH IN THE SHOWER.` → `DEEPER, TO THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard, he says, that it was said, thou shalt not kill. But I say unto you: whoever is angry with his brother is in danger of judgment. And whoever calls him raca, an insult usually explained as Aramaic for empty-head, is in danger too. It's the first of several times in this chapter Jesus says ye have heard, but I say unto you. He isn't canceling the commandment. He's following it back to its root. Murder starts somewhere: in contempt, in the name you call someone, in the grudge you feed. Then a small, practical story. In the King James Bible: "Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Picture it. You've traveled to the temple with a gift to offer. You're at the altar, and you remember that someone has something against you. Not that you're angry with them: they're angry with you. Leave the gift right there, Jesus says. Go. Make it right. Then come back. The Greek word is diallasso: to be reconciled, to make things up with someone. Your neighbor isn't separate from your worship. Christians say God cares about both, and here the neighbor comes first.

segments.voice: Let one face come to mind: someone you're angry with, or, like the story's twist, someone who has something against you, and notice the anger without feeding it. You don't have to fix everything today; just picture what leaving the gift and going might look like: a knock on a door, a call, I'm sorry for my part. If it isn't safe to reach out, simply let the anger rest, and if you pray, you can bring that person with you into your prayer.
Anger. Jesus follows thou shalt not kill back to its root, and says: before your gift, go and be reconciled.
Your line: reconcile first. The gift can wait at the altar while you make it right. Day two hundred forty-three, done.

244.title: The heart's look (Matthew 5:27–30)
244.hook: faithfulness starts in the eyes and the heart
244.howItsDone: Christians speak of guarding the heart and the eyes; in the Orthodox tradition this is called watchfulness, and some Christians examine what they've looked at and longed for in daily or weekly self-examination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anger, and a gift left at the altar while you go and make peace. Your line was reconcile first.

Every marriage, every friendship, every promise has a moment before the moment. Long before anyone does anything, there's a look that lingers. A daydream you keep returning to. A thought you feed instead of letting go. Nobody else can see it. It feels private and harmless. Jesus has followed thou shalt not kill back to anger. Now he takes another of the Ten Commandments and follows it back to the eyes.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE THE MOMENT.` → `A LOOK THAT LINGERS.` → `BACK TO THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, thou shalt not commit adultery. Then, in the King James Bible: "But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." This isn't about noticing that someone is attractive. The Greek phrase means looking at someone in order to desire them: a look with a purpose, fed on purpose. And the verb for lust, epithumeo, is the same word the Greek Old Testament uses in the commandment against coveting: thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's wife. So Jesus joins two commandments: the act and the wanting, the body and the heart. Faithfulness doesn't start at the door of a hotel room. It starts in what you let your eyes and your imagination rest on. Then a startling image: if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away. If your right hand does, cut it off. Christian tradition reads this as vivid exaggeration, the way a teacher makes a point unforgettable, not as a literal instruction. It means: take this seriously. Be willing to cut off what feeds the wrong thing, whether an app, a habit, a late-night conversation or a way of looking. The same logic reaches far beyond marriage. Envy, greed and resentment start the same way, with a look that lingers and gets fed. What you keep looking at, you start to want. What you want, you start to become.

segments.voice: Think about where your eyes go when you're bored or tired: which feeds, which screens, which faces, which store windows, and notice one kind of looking that leaves you emptier, more envious or less faithful to someone. Then picture the next hour, and your eyes resting somewhere else when that pull comes: the sky, a book, the person in front of you. If you pray, you can ask for a faithful heart.

Your line: faithful in the heart. Long before the act, there's the look. That's day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: Let your yes be yes (Matthew 5:33–37)
245.hook: no oaths needed if your word is plain
245.howItsDone: Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians affirm rather than swear in court, while many Christians take oaths in court or at ordination and try to keep ordinary promises as seriously as sworn ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, epithumeo: a look fed on purpose. Your line was faithful in the heart.

I swear. I promise. Honestly. To be fair. Trust me. Listen to how often people add a little booster to make their words count more. I swear I'll call you back. Honestly, I'm fine. Here's the odd thing: the more people use them, the more they suggest that without them, their words might not be true. If I have to say honestly, what was the rest? Next in the sermon, Jesus takes on the biggest booster of his world: the oath.
screen: `I SWEAR. HONESTLY. TRUST ME.` → `WORDS WITH BOOSTERS.` → `THE BIGGEST BOOSTER: THE OATH.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard, he says, that you shall not break your oaths, but keep what you've sworn to the Lord. That was the law: if you swore by God, you had to keep it. But people had found loopholes. Swear by heaven, or the earth, or Jerusalem, or your own head, and maybe it didn't count quite as much. Jesus closes every loophole. Heaven is God's throne. The earth is his footstool. Jerusalem is the city of the great King. You can't even make one hair of your head white or black. Everything you swear by belongs to God anyway. Then, in the King James Bible: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." The point isn't a new rule about courtrooms. There shouldn't be two kinds of speech: sworn words you keep, and ordinary words you don't. If your yes always means yes, you never need to swear. The letter of James repeats it: let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay. Christians live this out in different ways. Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians refuse to swear oaths at all, and affirm instead; that's one reason the United States Constitution lets a president swear or affirm. Many other Christians take oaths in court or in office, reading Jesus as teaching everyday honesty, not banning every oath. Both take the heart of it seriously: a plain word, kept. Look back at this week: peacemakers, the persecuted, salt and light, the Torah fulfilled, anger, the heart's look, and now a plain yes. Each goes deeper than the rule.
screen: `LOOPHOLES: HEAVEN, EARTH, JERUSALEM.` · `EVERYTHING BELONGS TO GOD.` · `ONE KIND OF SPEECH.` · `SWEAR OR AFFIRM.` · then, large: `YEA, YEA; NAY, NAY.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day or two: where did you say yes and mean maybe, say I'm fine and mean something else, or add I swear or honestly? No guilt, just notice. Then picture one conversation today where you say a plain yes or a plain no, and mean it, and if you pray, you can ask for a plain, true tongue.
Nai, the Greek word for yes, which Greeks still say today. Jesus closes the loopholes around oaths and asks for one kind of speech: yea, yea; nay, nay.
Your line: yes means yes. A plain word, kept, needs no booster. A week of the sermon, done.
